title: Approval gates and escalation
summary: An approval gate pauses an agent action until a person decides. Tier actions by reversibility and reach, gate the risky tiers, define who reviews and what happens on timeout, and bind each approval to the request it answers.
useIf: An agent can take actions with external, irreversible or high-value effects.
avoidIf: Every tool call would need approval: reviewers will rubber-stamp, so tier the actions first.

explain.md: Start by **tiering actions** on four dials: reversibility, blast radius, data sensitivity and external visibility. A read-only internal action runs freely. A reversible internal write runs with logging and sampled review. An external or hard-to-undo action needs one approval. An irreversible, high-value or regulated action needs two reviewers and evidence. Tier by **action class and arguments**, not by tool name: a refund of 5 and a refund of 5,000 are different risks, and a second tool that sends the same email must fall in the same tier.

In Microsoft Agent Framework a Python tool opts in with `@tool(approval_mode="always_require")`, and the run result exposes `user_input_requests`. In .NET you wrap the function in `ApprovalRequiredAIFunction` and the response carries `ToolApprovalRequestContent`. By default a local approval response authorises a call only when it matches a pending request recorded in the same `AgentSession`; `disable_approval_response_binding` opts out and can let a fabricated or replayed response approve a privileged call [[r16]]. Define **escalation** too: triggers (policy hit, low confidence, novelty, amount, anomaly), a named queue with an SLA, and a **fail-closed** default so an unanswered request means the action does not run.

explain.title: A tiered approval path
explain.alt: The agent proposes an action, a policy check routes low tiers straight to execution and high tiers to an approval queue. A reviewer approves to execute or rejects, and timeouts do not execute. Everything is logged.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  A[Agent proposes action] --> P{Policy check}
  P -->|tier 0 or 1| X[Execute and log]
  P -->|tier 2 or 3| Q[Approval queue]
  Q --> R[Reviewer sees evidence]
  R -->|approve| X
  R -->|reject or timeout| N[Do not execute]

explain.title: Opting a tool into approval (illustrative)
explain.caption: Pair the built-in hook with policy code that decides which calls need it.

whereToUse: Outbound email, messaging and publishing actions
Any session that combines untrusted input, sensitive data and external effects [[r23]]

use: The action is irreversible or externally visible
Prompt injection could steer the agent into it
Amounts or data sensitivity cross a threshold
A regulator or contract expects a human decision
avoid: Gating reads and trivial reversible writes
Approvals with no evidence, authority or time to decide
flips: The reviewer queue exceeds its SLA: raise thresholds or add reviewers, never auto-approve
Actions become reversible with an undo: move down a tier
A new tool exposes the same effect: classify it in the same tier

pitfalls.symptom: A tool is gated but the same effect still happens
pitfalls.cause: Approval is attached to one tool, and another tool or path reaches the same outcome
pitfalls.fix: Gate by action class and arguments, and test alternative paths

pitfalls.symptom: Requests pile up and approvals are rushed
pitfalls.cause: Too many low-risk actions reach the queue
pitfalls.fix: Tier, raise thresholds for reversible actions, and measure catch rate on seeded bad items
Fail closed: no decision means no action, with a visible expiry and retry path

pitfalls.symptom: A fabricated approval executes a call
pitfalls.cause: Approval binding to the pending request was disabled
pitfalls.fix: Keep the default binding and bind to request, user and session [[r16]]

scenarios.title: Twelve tools, three of them dangerous
scenarios.situation: An internal agent has twelve tools. Eight read data, three write reversible internal records, and one sends payments up to a large limit.
unknowns: What is the payment threshold for two-person approval?
scenarios.question: How do you set gates?

options.name: Tier by action: reads free, internal writes logged with sampled review, payments gated by amount with two-person approval above a threshold
options.why: Effort goes where harm is irreversible, and the queue stays small enough to be reviewed carefully.

options.name: Approve every tool call
options.why: Eight read tools flood the queue, and reviewers start clicking through.
options.tradeoff: Right for a tiny tool set that is all high-risk.

options.name: Gate only the payment tool by name
options.tradeoff: Misses effects reachable by other tools and amounts that matter at lower values.

flips.if: Another tool can trigger the same payment indirectly
flips.then: Gate by effect, not by tool.

scenarios.takeaway: Tier by effect and arguments, not by tool name.

scenarios.title: No reviewer at 3 a.m.
scenarios.situation: Overnight, an agent proposes a high-value action and the approval queue has no active reviewer for six hours.
constraints: A rota exists but is thin overnight
unknowns: Can the action wait until morning?
Is there an on-call path for urgent cases?
scenarios.question: What happens to the request?

options.name: Fail closed: hold the request, notify on-call for urgent cases and expire visibly
options.why: No decision means no irreversible action, and the owner still gets a path for urgent work.
options.tradeoff: Delay and a possible missed business window.

options.name: Auto-approve after one hour
options.why: It turns the gate into a delay, and attackers can wait out the timer.
options.tradeoff: Acceptable only for reversible, low-value actions.

options.name: Let the agent run with a smaller amount
options.tradeoff: Splitting amounts can be gamed and changes the business outcome.

flips.if: The action is reversible with an undo
flips.then: Run it, log it and review in the morning.

scenarios.takeaway: A gate that fails open is not a gate.

scenarios.title: Untrusted input, private data, external send
scenarios.situation: An agent reads inbound customer emails, can search private account data, and can send replies. A crafted email could steer it.
constraints: All three Rule of Two properties are needed
unknowns: Can a leg be removed, such as sending without human review?
scenarios.question: What control do you add first?

options.name: Require human approval on outbound replies that include private data
options.why: The Rule of Two says approval is the fallback when untrusted input, sensitive access and external effects are all needed.

options.name: Rely on a system prompt that says to ignore instructions in emails
options.why: It is a probabilistic control and attackers bypass classifiers.
options.tradeoff: Useful as one layer, never the only one.

options.name: Remove private data access and reply from templates
options.tradeoff: Reduces what the agent can do for customers.

flips.if: Replies can be restricted to non-sensitive templates

flips.then: Gate by data sensitivity and recipient novelty.

scenarios.takeaway: If you cannot remove a trifecta leg, put a person on the exit.

quiz.q: Put the approval path in order.
items: Policy classifies tier by action and arguments
quiz.explain: Classification precedes review, execution follows an explicit decision, and the audit record closes the loop. A timeout leads to no execution, not to approval.

quiz.q: Why does Agent Framework bind an approval response to a pending request in the same session by default?
options: So a fabricated or replayed response cannot approve a privileged call
To store approvals in the model
quiz.explain: The default binding stops replayed or invented approvals. `disable_approval_response_binding` removes that protection [[r16]]. Speed and storage are unrelated.

quiz.q: A tool needs approval but the reviewer queue is behind. Which response is acceptable?
options: Add reviewers or raise thresholds for reversible actions
quiz.explain: Capacity and tiering fix backlog. Auto-approve and removing logs weaken the control and accountability.

flashcards.front: How do you declare approval in Agent Framework?
flashcards.back: Python: `@tool(approval_mode="always_require")` with `user_input_requests` on the result. .NET: wrap in `ApprovalRequiredAIFunction`, response carries `ToolApprovalRequestContent`.

flashcards.front: Why tier by action class, not tool name?
flashcards.back: Risk depends on effect and arguments. Another tool or a larger amount can reach the same harm past a per-tool flag.
Fail closed: no decision means no action. Expire visibly and give urgent cases an on-call path.
